title: The remarkable legacy of the K6/ODC mouse: mechanisms of polyamine-promoted tumorigenesis revealed

sections.abstract: Using the well-studied two-stage model of skin carcinogenesis, the first transgenic mouse with targeted expression of a polyamine metabolic enzyme was generated 30 years ago. Ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), a key regulating enzyme of polyamine biosynthesis, was constitutively expressed in the outer root sheath cells of hair follicles near the bulge stem cell niche using a keratin 6 promoter in K6/ODC mice. Early studies using K6/ODC mice demonstrated that polyamines play an essential role in the early promotional phase of skin tumorigenesis. Treatment with inhibitors of ODC activity blocked the formation of skin tumors and caused the rapid regression of existing tumors. We review how use of the K6/ODC mouse has shown that elevated polyamines in epithelial cells stimulate proliferation and invasiveness, recruit stem cells, alter chromatin remodeling and cell signaling leading to metabolic reprogramming, increase vascularization, activate underlying fibroblasts, and have powerful effects on immune cell function, all contributing to the development and progression of tumors.
sections.introduction:
Nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) is a major worldwide health concern due to its high incidence, associated medical costs, morbidity, and cosmetic defects resulting from current treatments. There are two major types of NMSC including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) that account for 70% and 25% of all diagnosed skin cancers, respectively. Skin cancers are the most common of all types of cancer in the United States with 5.4 million NMSC cases diagnosed each year (Ciuciulete et al. 2022 ).

The mouse skin model of two-stage skin carcinogenesis has been a widely used model for the study of the sequential and stepwise development of skin tumors and has provided an important instrumental framework for defining many current concepts regarding human neoplasia (Yuspa 1986 , Abel et al. 2009 ). Mice are initiated with a low subthreshold topical dose of a carcinogen such as 7,12-dimethylbenz(a)anthracene (DMBA) which results in H-ras gene mutations but no tumor formation. However, subsequent, repetitive treatments with tumor promoting agents such as 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA) or wounding lead to the development of skin tumors. Tumor promoting agents such as TPA are not mutagenic but cause chronic hyperplasia, edema, and a robust inflammatory response in the skin, resulting in a neoplastic lesion that contains one or more genetic lesions. Because tumors can be elicited in carcinogen-initiated skin even with long intervals between initiation and promotion, it is believed that carcinogen target cells in the skin are long lived, slowly cycling stem cells found in the bulge region within the outer sheath of hair follicles (Gerdes and Yuspa 2005 , Singh et al. 2012 , Morris et al. 2000 , Owens and Watt 2003 ).

Elevated levels of polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, and spermine) have long been associated with tumorigenesis. Tightly regulated metabolism of polyamines is critical for cell survival and normal skin homeostasis, and these controls are dysregulated during tumor formation resulting in constitutively elevated levels of polyamines in tumors compared to normal skin. More than 50 years ago, use of the DMBA-TPA skin carcinogenesis mouse model demonstrated that a key enzyme in polyamine biosynthesis, ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) is transiently induced following topical treatment with tumor promoting agents (O’Brien 1976 ). In order to determine whether the induction of ODC by tumor promoting agents is essential for skin tumorigenesis in mouse skin, a keratin 6-driven ODC transgenic mouse model in which ODC is constitutively expressed in the outer root sheath of hair follicles was generated (Megosh et al. 1995 ). In order to mimic the constitutively high levels of ODC activity in skin tumors, a premature stop codon at position 427 in the mouse ODC cDNA was placed downstream of the K6 promoter resulting in a carboxyl-truncated ODC protein with a much longer in vivo half-life than the full-length ODC protein (Ghoda et al. 1989 , Clifford et al. 1995 ). These sustained high levels of polyamine biosynthesis in K6/ODC mouse skin lead to hair loss beginning at 3 weeks of age when the second cycle of hair growth begins followed by the subsequent development of follicular dermal cysts (Megosh et al. 1995 , Soler et al. 1996 ). Treatment with the ODC inhibitor α-difluoromethylornithine (DFMO) prevented this hair loss in K6/ODC transgenic mice and reactivated hair growth in mice with complete hair loss, suggesting that ODC is an important regulator of hair follicle function (Soler et al. 1996 ).

This review describes how the use of the K6/ODC mouse model not only has demonstrated the essential role of polyamines in the early tumor promotion stages of tumorigenesis but also has revealed multiple ways in which polyamines regulate normal skin homeostasis and tissue remodeling including wound healing and tumor development. The K6/ODC mouse model has contributed to a better understanding of mechanisms by which polyamines affect multiple biological pathways leading to increased cellular proliferation, invasiveness, stem cell recruitment, angiogenesis, fibroblast activation, and changes in immune cell function. In addition to its impact in the cancer field, we describe how the K6/ODC mouse served as an important animal model for the recently identified human gain-of-function ODC genetic disorder (the Bachmann-Bupp syndrome) that facilitated a relatively quick treatment for these patients.
